title: US Secure Hash Algorithms (SHA and SHA-based HMAC and HKDF)
summary: This informational document reproduces the US Secure Hash Algorithms from Federal Information Processing Standards, along with SHA-based HMAC and HKDF. It provides reference code so others can implement and test them. These are widely used hash functions for security protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: A hash function squeezes any message down to a short fixed-length value in a way that is meant to be impossible to reverse or to fake. This memo describes the SHA family of such functions clearly, and prints the full source code for them and for two tools built on top, HMAC for proving a message came from someone who shares a secret key, and HKDF for turning one key into several.

questions: what is the difference between sha-256 and sha-512
subtitle: Complete reference implementations for the SHA family of hash functions, together with HMAC and HKDF, in C.

tldr.problem: An earlier RFC gave incomplete and occasionally inconsistent descriptions of the SHA hash functions, making it hard for implementers to produce code that matched the published standard.
tldr.mechanism: This memo restates the SHAs with corrected, self-contained descriptions and includes the full C source for SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, plus HMAC and HKDF built on them.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational reference: it obsoletes RFC 4634 and updates the algorithm description in RFC 3174, and implementers have used its code as the definition of the algorithms.

today: RFC 6234 is an Informational RFC published in May 2011. It obsoletes RFC 4634 and updates RFC 3174; the unit metadata lists no successor. Because it is a restatement of the published SHA standards, later work on stronger hash functions and on retiring SHA-1 does not flow through this RFC.

sections.title: Why a New SHA Specification
sections.content:
This memo provides a clear, consistent, and self-contained description of the SHA hash algorithms, their HMAC and HKDF applications, and a reference implementation of each in the C programming language. It arose because RFC 3174, which describes SHA-1, does not provide either a complete description of the algorithm or an implementation, and because RFC 4634 contained inconsistencies in the presentation of the algorithm descriptions and the source code.

The hashes covered are the SHA family specified by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in FIPS 180-3: SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. The applications are HMAC, the keyed-hash message authentication code, and HKDF, the extract-and-expand key derivation function from RFC 5869. The document updates the SHA-1 description in RFC 3174 and obsoletes RFC 4634.

Since the algorithms are already defined by the standards bodies, the source code in this memo is offered as a way to make the definitions precise rather than as a new standard. Implementers are free to write their own code so long as it produces the specified results.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier documents that described these hash functions were incomplete or inconsistent, so this one writes them out clearly and adds working code. The algorithms themselves come from the relevant standards; the value here is a description and reference code that implementers can rely on.

sections.title: How the Hashes Work
sections.content:
Every hash function here processes a message in fixed-size blocks and produces a fixed-size digest. SHA-1 and SHA-256 use a 512-bit block and 32-bit words; SHA-224 is the same structure with a different initial state and a truncated result; SHA-384 and SHA-512 use a 1024-bit block and 64-bit words, with SHA-384 being a truncated SHA-512. Messages longer than these architectures can represent are not supported: the maximum message length is 2 to the 64th minus one bits for the 32-bit designs and 2 to the 128th minus one bits for the 64-bit designs.

Each algorithm begins with a fixed initial hash value, applies a sequence of rounds built from additions, bitwise operations and rotations to each block, and outputs the resulting state as the digest. SHA-1 produces 160 bits, SHA-224 produces 224, SHA-256 produces 256, SHA-384 produces 384 and SHA-512 produces 512. The messages and digests are treated as sequences of bytes in network order.

Because the round functions are simple and fast, these hashes are cheap to compute, which is exactly what a hash function needs to be. The security comes from the apparent impossibility of finding two different messages with the same digest or of working backward from a digest to its message.
sections.plainLanguage: Each function chews through a message in fixed-size chunks, mixing each chunk into a running value with simple arithmetic and bit operations, and finally prints that value as a short code. Different versions produce different lengths of code, and the two families differ in how much they process at once.

sections.title: HMAC and HKDF
sections.content:
HMAC, the keyed-hash message authentication code defined in RFC 2104, combines a secret key with a hash function to produce a value that proves both that a message is unchanged and that the sender knows the key. It can be built on any of the SHA functions, and the memo supplies a reference implementation for each. Unlike a bare hash, which anyone can compute, an HMAC can only be produced by someone who holds the key, which is what makes it useful for protecting messages in transit.

HKDF, the HMAC-based extract-and-expand key derivation function from RFC 5869, uses HMAC to turn some existing source of key material into one or more cryptographically strong keys of the lengths an application needs. It works in two stages: an extract stage that condenses the input into a fixed-length pseudorandom key, and an expand stage that stretches that key into as many output bytes as required. This lets systems start from a single shared secret or a Diffie-Hellman value and still derive separate keys for different purposes.

Both applications rely on the underlying hashes being collision resistant and preimage resistant, so all of the caveats about choosing a strong hash apply to them as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Two tools are built on the hashes. One, HMAC, mixes in a secret key so that a short code shows a message was not tampered with and really came from someone who holds the key. The other, HKDF, uses HMAC to turn one secret into several strong keys of whatever sizes an application needs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo notes that hash functions of this kind represent a trade-off between speed and strength and that they have stood up to heavy scrutiny, while cautioning that no hash function has been proven secure. The goal of these functions is that finding a message with a given digest, or finding two messages with the same digest, should be computationally infeasible, so that a digest can stand in for a message wherever a compact or hidden representation is needed.

SHA-1 is singled out as the weakest of the family and is treated as the one whose security rests on the oldest and most heavily examined design; later members of the family were built to provide the same style of guarantee with longer outputs. The number of rounds and the fixed initial values are not tunable: implementations must use the values the standard specifies or the results will not match. Because the code provided is reference code rather than a hardened product, applications that need strong protection should pair these hashes with the keyed modes, HMAC and HKDF, rather than relying on a bare digest for authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: These functions are fast and well studied but not proven safe, so the memo is careful about how much weight to put on them. It calls the oldest member of the family the weakest, and it warns that you should not use a plain hash to prove a message is genuine; you should use the keyed version instead.
